story_text.value:
Compose Unstyled is a collection of fully accessible, unstyled components that you can use to build your own components using Jetpack Compose and Kotlin.

I started the library because I found Jetpack Compose too coupled to Material. I wanted to build apps with my own look and feel.

2 years and 1221 commits later, the project is used by companies such as Perplexity, Warner Bros and Expo.

All components are unopinionated and can be styled using just plain Modifiers. All the UX is handled for you, so that you can focus on your product instead of trying to figure out how to build Bottom Sheets and dialogs.

title.value: Show HN: Compose Unstyled – Unstyled Components for Jetpack Compose and CMP

story_text.value:
I've been using Claude code to finish up some projects that were on hold for a while. I've been doing this in my laptop, keeping the changes local. In one session I was offered $100 usd credits to let Claude connect and work in one of my GitHub projects directly. So I chose aimAndShoot, a neural evolution game from 2019. It catched some bugs and introduced improvements. I told it I was going to post about this experience on hackernews and lo and behold, the topic was already in it's training data. It knew about the project and the fact that I hadn't addressed the feedback it got. Anyhow, I asked it to address the comments on the topic and here's the result.

Live game is here: https://victorribeiro.com/aimAndShoot/

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

We built CropGuide for people who don't code (or use platforms that don't allow custom code) but do want to improve the quality of images uploaded by their users.

To make that possible, we've built an admin tool where you configure your image requirements. Then you add a script tag to the page with the file upload field, either a standard file input or something more exotic powered by a library, and that's it.

The script catches images before they're added to the file input and lets the user edit them. Once edited, CropGuide places the resulting image back in the file input and everything continues as normal.

We really wanted to stay away from storing or processing images on our servers, so all of this happens client-side. Only the image requirements are fetched from the server.

Of course we're sharing because we're excited about having built and launched something new. Now it's fingers crossed that we can get some traction.

Would love to hear what you think!

title.value: Show HN: Client-side image cropping for any file input, without coding

story_text.value:
I've been working on Stećak, a lightweight terminal emulator inspired by Ghostty and Alacritty.

The idea came from stećci (singular: stećak), monumental medieval stone tombstones found across Bosnia and Herzegovina and neighboring parts of the Balkans. They have distinctive geometric carvings, symbols, and shapes that I've always found fascinating.

I wanted to build a terminal that takes inspiration from that heritage while remaining focused on what matters in a terminal emulator: simplicity, speed, and a lightweight experience.

The project is still a work in progress, and I'm sharing it to get feedback from people who know terminals and systems programming better than I do.

GitHub: https://github.com/alminisl/stecak

I'd love feedback on the technical direction, what you'd expect from a modern lightweight terminal, and whether there's anything interesting here beyond the visual identity.

title.value: Show HN: Stećak – a lightweight terminal inspired by Bosnian medieval tombstones

story_text.value:
I used to HATE public speaking.

But then I joined debate, and through the constant cycle of practicing, messing up in front of everyone, and getting feedback, I improved to the point where I was winning debate competitions.

Most people never get the kind of feedback I got through debate.

So I built SpeakUp, an iOS app that does it for you. The idea is simple. Every day you get a 1-minute question (either on interviews, everyday conversations, or debate), and you record your answer. You then get feedback on things like pausing, pacing, filler words, intonation, and more! (And there are modes for further practice too!)

title.value: Show HN: SpeakUp – iOS app for feedback on your speaking (fillers, pauses, etc.)

story_text.value:
Voice AI industry still uses transcripts to determine the emotions of the user.

So when me and my friend were discussing about this we got the known limitations of transcriptions is that it doesn't capture the user's emotion from audio. Like, "I'm frustrated with your service" reads the same whether calm or angry.

Then I thought, why can't the decision model be tested for this to get quicker decisions on the go, knowing the limitation that it can't accept the audio file directly? So I thought of converting it to a pictorial representation and then submitting it to the clef-flash [a cheaper option]. Although the results are not too exciting, I would say it is just starting, and we can fine-tune the decision model for the same use case, and it can help a lot in several scenarios.

Worth giving it a try and checkout on your own voice.

title.value: Show HN: SpectroMood, speech emotion detection with a decision model

story_text.value:
About 10 years ago, I attended a presentation by someone who had compiled existing engineering reports to describe the impact of a major earthquake on infrastructure in British Columbia. It was really striking, and it has stayed in the back of my mind ever since.

I am now the point of contact for downtown Vancouver in the French community's emergency network, and it drives me nuts that most people I talk to have no emergency kit at home and basically no water.

People are shocked, or in denial, when I mention that it could take weeks to restore electricity and that they will have to rely on their own food and water for at least several days.

So I decided to build a public-facing site that compiles existing information, as a way to lay out the facts and help convince people, instead of hearing back that "the army will come" or that "there are emergency food reserves" (there aren't).

I see this as a citizen initiative, with one main message: go buy some water and canned food, it's your civic duty.

I relied on AI agents to compile the information, which is spread across hundreds of reports. With different levels of validation, plus my own review, I am confident the information is reliable, even if some details may not be fully up to date. The process took 2–3 weeks, alongside work, a toddler and a baby!

I'm posting it here because: 1) I'm curious to get feedback and suggestions. 2) Many HN readers are on the West Coast or in other seismic areas, so even if you're not in Vancouver, the general recommendations may be of interest. Be smart: buy some food and water.

Cheers

Thomas
